acceptedReports.program: Worker organizing, wage enforcement, industry policy and member support

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/la-gwc-root-acceptance-20261005.md; original 2024 return/narrative checked and 139 independent arithmetic checks across 27 corrected scenarios.

what: Garment Worker Center organizes low-wage garment workers and operates a wage-theft and retaliation clinic in Los Angeles.
It provides rights education, self-help, referrals and representation in Labor Commissioner hearings alongside worker leadership and member support.
It is developing a Justice Campus and advocating for stronger enforcement and garment-sector job quality.
strengths: Original return narrative reports wages and penalties collected rather than pricing outreach as completed outcomes.
Trusted representation can help workers turn existing legal rights into payments; current clinic hours establish ongoing access.
Original finances and the capital campaign expose costs, public funding and the distinction between operations and future expansion.
reservations: Paid household count, net recovery, alternative enforcement, baseline resources and payer incidence remain unmeasured.
Unrestricted gifts may replace other funding or support capital and organizing rather than additional wage collection.
Retaliation, displacement, transfer losses and unresolved audit/capital evidence can offset gains; this is a conditional partial comparison.

sections.what:
This report covers Garment Worker Center, EIN 81-0622327. Its [clinic](https://garmentworkercenter.org/wage-clinic/) provides consultations, self-help and representation for wage theft and retaliation. Worker organizing, youth leadership, member support and industry development are substantive parts of the recipient, not overhead to be discarded.

The [current industry campaign](https://garmentworkercenter.org/lagfip/) seeks implementation and resources for LA garment-sector development. Its [recent report](https://garmentworkercenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Building-a-Sustainable-and-Equitable-Garment-Industry-in-California-RBG.pdf) describes continued noncompliance and economic vulnerability. The report's 18,408 apparel-manufacturing employees and the homepage's broader 45,000-worker figure have different coverage and are not treated as current beneficiaries caused by a gift.
sections.monitoring:
The [2024 return narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO) reports 194 workers assisted with wage claims and approximately $878,000 of wages and penalties collected. It separately reports 135 workers/youth in training, 6,250 outreach contacts and 191 support cases. These categories may overlap; no contact or workshop automatically earns health credit.

Collections are a realized financial outcome, but still do not reveal which dollars would have arrived without GWC, whether recipients lost benefits or earnings, or how a new gift changes capacity. Future measurement should follow net household resources, timing, retaliation, worker residence and non-overlapping injury outcomes. Policy wins should be assessed against already funded implementation.
sections.qualitative: Existing SB62 and DIR wage enforcement remain the baseline. Additional trusted representation may improve collections, but the sources do not identify next-dollar causal recovery. We replace the initial 0.01-QALY-per-$6,000 shortcut with direct signed consumption welfare and a central judgment of zero separately counted clinical QALYs. This avoids adding the same material-hardship or stress outcome twice; it does not establish that health effects are absent. Safety, organizing, deterrence, jobs and campus effects remain unquantified. The independent clinical sensitivity is hypothetical, not derived from income.
sections.cost:
The conditional central estimate is **$23.36 million per better life**: ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents. A $10,000 gift normalization produces zero separately counted clinical QALYs and 0.00428138 signed consumption-equivalent years. The initial $88.14 million health-only illustration remains a diagnostic. The change reflects direct income accounting and full claimant/counterparty costs, not measured improvement in the organization.

Full recognized annual recipient resources are $2,974,158: $2,820,655 in Part IX plus $153,503 of rental expenses separately netted from revenue. All programs and support remain charged; there is no favorable campaign carveout. The state-funded campus acquisition is already in the baseline, not wholly a one-year operating expense or permanently free capital. Public enforcement, capital services and unrecognized donated work remain additional unpriced social costs. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990)

The reported $878,000 in collected wages and penalties anchors 100 judged receipt-household units, not 194 confirmed paid households. Equal $8,780 gross awards, a $30,000 disposable-resource baseline and 75% retention after taxes/benefit losses are assumptions, not measured household data. The resulting $6,585 receipt is netted jointly with $300 of claimant time, travel, forgone earnings and retaliation costs before log valuation. One representative adult-equivalent is counted per modeled household; additional family members are not multiplied in. A one-time award supports one consumption year after a one-year delay. [Original program narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO)

Half the recoveries are judged additional to public enforcement, other representation and employer payment. In the other outcome no additional receipt arrives, but claimant costs remain. The other 94 assisted-equivalent units also incur full costs without a credited payment, independently of recovery probability. Treating the reported 194 assisted workers as distinct resource units is a judgment tested against household overlap. A separate 50% funding response accounts for replacement funding and operating/capital allocation. No priced staff tranche verifies a linear ordinary-gift response.

Restitution transfers resources from payers. The model charges the full incremental gross transfer to 50 disjoint counterparty units with a judged $100,000 resource baseline and 50% local incidence. Worker residence is judged 95% local. Payer incidence, tax offsets and household baselines are unknown; legal liability does not erase their signed welfare loss. Positive overlap discounts apply only to worker gains, not costs. Out-of-boundary payer losses are not included in the LA headline, so it is not a complete global welfare estimate. [Comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/)

The 27 scenarios retain the same financial ledger when clinical benefit is null. Concentrating the same award total among ten recipients raises the reference price to $95.41 million; counting only 100 claimant units gives $19.94 million. Lower collection additionality, poorer fully local payers or large retaliation/displacement costs can make net welfare negative. Complete funding replacement gives zero; independent gift-induced engagement costs can survive that failure. An unknown-incidence scenario has no combined price. Two-year smoothing spreads the same award and costs instead of repeating annual collections. These are judgment sensitivities, not confidence bounds. Neither the current reference nor the frozen initial model is a complete portfolio valuation or a verified donation offer.
sections.funding:
The latest return records $9,257,935 in government grants and $10,060,845 total revenue. Net assets were $7,653,173, but cash was only $204,063 and net land/buildings/equipment were $10,468,795; net assets are not an unrestricted cash runway. The return does not separate donor restrictions using the usual FASB categories.

The [Justice Campus page](https://garmentworkercenter.org/justice-campus/) confirms a state-funded 2024 property purchase and describes renovations in stages. These are plans, not completed additional clinic capacity. [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO) also says the emergency hardship fund closed after reduced donations and grants. The [2023 narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202433189349310008/IRS990ScheduleO) identifies the DIR wage-claim pilot partnership. These details show both public support and real allocation tradeoffs.

The central 50% funding response is a judgment that a proportional resource increment produces half the corresponding collection capacity after replacement and delays. New unrestricted gifts could instead fund capital, worker leadership or support services, so this operating scenario is conditional. No restricted best-program donation, outreach or payment is assumed.

model.costScope: Full recipient gross annual cost; priced health limited to a wage-recovery component.
model.geographicAttribution: OMB23-01 LA MSA:Los Angeles+Orange; Inland Empire/Ventura excluded. g=.95 worker residence and payerLocalShare=.5 are unmeasured. allPopulationQalys equals locally quantified clinical health; not statewide outcomes.
model.formula: effort=gift/C*b. Paid/failure mutually exclusive branches: people*effort*a and people*effort*(1-a). Paid net=(R/people*retention*positiveShare-workerCost)/years; failure net=-workerCost/years. Disjoint payers lose R/payerPeople/years. Production CG=.5*people*discountedYears*log1p(net/baseline)*causal*local. reportPrice adds once. Clinical=effort*g*(people*clinicalPerPerson*clinicalAttribution-clinicalHarm)/1.03^delay; central clinical0.
model.counterfactual: Existing SB62, DIR public enforcement, other advocates and employer payments continue. State-funded2024 campus acquisition baseline. New donation may support operations,capital or organizing; no restricted best-program allocation assumed.
model.attribution: $878000 collected aggregate,not194 paid workers.100 distinct household units with equal awards is judgment. a=.5 recovery additionality versus alternative enforcement; b=.5 marginal gift responsiveness. Same-household positives minus full negatives before log; unsuccessful claim costs remain. Payer losses match full additional gross transfer. No wages of extra survivors or recurring salary. All194 judged claimant household-equivalent units bear full costs; other94 incur costs independent of wage a. Not194 confirmed households. Overlap100claimant and concentrated10paid sensitivities test deduplication and Jensen concavity. Nonlocal payer harms outside LA headline remain unpriced, not absent world harms.
model.uncertainty: Conditional source-anchored priors, not identified causal organizational effectiveness. Clinical central0 removes arbitrary cash-derived health duplication. Whole-portfolio health/resource effects remain unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional collected wages/penalties translated into net household consumption after tax/benefit/work costs, plus full payer/counterparty losses. Current sources lack actual paid-household/distribution ledger.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full recipient gross annual cost; priced health limited to a wage-recovery component.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: g=.95 is a judgment about LA/Orange resident share of represented workers; employment in LA is not proof of residence.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: Rnet=R*a*b; E=Rnet/k; Q=E*q*g/1.03; Price10=10*C/Q. R=878000,a=.5,b=.5,k=6000,q=.01,g=.95,C=2974158. Qportfolio=Q+Qother-H, with Qother unknown. Safety skeleton Qs=Nnew*injuryRate*.094*transfer*healthPerInjury*duration*g; Nnew and local injury bridge unknown.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Existing law, DIR representation, other advocates and employer payments continue. a discounts collections that would occur anyway; b concerns future resource responsiveness, not another collection probability.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: R is collected wages and penalties, not filed claims. k defines resource-equivalent units, not an observed household size or number of people. No lifetime income or mortality extrapolation and no duplicate counting of ongoing wages.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Health conversion is explicitly subjective and contested by modern randomized income evidence. Conditional component best estimate only; zero, harm and omitted policy value remain possible.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Central Rnet=$219,500; 36.5833 equivalents of $6,000 in incremental resources. Each receives a 0.01-QALY finite one-year prior before residence and delivery discount. These are modeled resource equivalents, not observed additional workers.

inputs.name: C
inputs.unit: USD gross annual recipient cost
inputs.rationale: Part IX plus $153503 rental expense.

inputs.name: R
inputs.unit: USD collected wages and penalties
inputs.rationale: Approximate organization-reported amount, not independently audited causal effect.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: counterfactual collection attribution
inputs.rationale: Half would not otherwise be collected or are accelerated equivalently; test .1–.9.

inputs.name: b
inputs.unit: proportional funding response
inputs.rationale: Contracts, capital allocation and other donors can replace resources; test .1–.8.

inputs.name: k
inputs.unit: USD net-resource equivalent
inputs.rationale: Normalization for a finite health prior, not observed income threshold; test 3000–12000.

inputs.name: q
inputs.unit: QALY per resource equivalent over one year
inputs.rationale: Modest hardship-related health prior, not a cash-trial estimate; test 0–.05.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: LA/Orange residence fraction
inputs.rationale: Local clinic supports concentration; test .8–1.

inputs.name: d
inputs.unit: one-year delivery discount
inputs.rationale: No repeated lifetime benefit.

inputs.name: Qother
inputs.unit: non-overlapping portfolio QALYs
inputs.rationale: Safety, organizing, services and campus effects need separate causal measurement.
